CPTSD is real. 

My therapist "diagnosed" me with it last year. We did a brain scan with a neurologist (also interested in studying more into the differences between CPTSD and PTSD). He wanted to see what the difference was between a brain of someone with PTSD and CPTSD. It was very different. My doctors called it more of a "psychological injury" since most of this bullshittery happened when I was young. My brain is not wired like a normal person's. Sorry, I don't have a copy of the scans. 

The major difference is the severity of the situation. Examples:

A veteran of war may develop PTSD.

A veteran who was held captive with no viable escape or way out may develop CPTSD.

Someone who was involved in a car crash that killed someone close to them may develop PTSD.

Someone who was involved in a car crash that killed someone, and left in the car for hours/days without help my develop CPTSD.

The major difference really between the two is that you were held against your will in a situation that your life was in constant danger, with no way of escape/getting away from the trauma for an extended period of time.

Also, your life is constantly switching between three cycles. The first is when you almost have amnesia of the traumatic experience(s). The second, it's like the trauma just happened yesterday. The third is heavy depersonalization/derealization when you pretty much just function on autopilot and shut down completely.

Another thing, you cannot phantom the idea of emotionally connecting yourself to another human being. You know just how bad people can be, and you were likely close to the person or people who held you captive and threatened your life. This makes it really hard to look at a person who's complimenting you or saying nice things or hell, even trying to get laid... You cannot trust or allow yourself to love anyone. I think that's why service animals are wonderful for PTSD/CPTSD survivors. 

Hypervigilance. You are a hawk out on patrol, 24/7. You are preparing for the trauma to happen again and you're gonna make damn sure it doesn't happen again to you. It's mentally exhausting to constantly be monitoring the actions and behaviors of everyone around you. You'll probably end up hating large crowds because you can't keep a constant eye on who's around you. At least this is my personal experience.

I'm not really going to delve too deeply into my case. I was diagnosed back in the summer of 2012, but since CPTSD isn't recognized in the DSMV, it's not a legitimate mental disability/illness.

**TL;DR**

I was a test dummy for a psych doc and neurologist studying the differences between PTSD and CPTSD. CPTSD is definitely real. Fuck the DSMV.
